title: have and have got
subtitle: I have / I've got
summary: Use have or have got for possession, and have (never have got) for things you do, like have breakfast or have a shower.

lesson.heading: have and have got: no difference in meaning
lesson.text: For possession, relationships, illnesses, appointments etc. you can use **have** or **have got**. There is no difference in meaning.

examples.text: They **have** a new car. or They**'ve got** a new car.
Lisa **has** two brothers. or Lisa **has got** two brothers.
I **have** a headache. or I**'ve got** a headache.
Our house **has** a small garden. or Our house **has got** a small garden.
I **have** a driving lesson tomorrow. or I**'ve got** a driving lesson tomorrow.

lesson.heading: No continuous, and had in the past
lesson.text: With these meanings (possession etc.) we do not use continuous forms (I'm having etc.). For the past we use **had**, usually without got.

examples.text: We're enjoying our holiday. **We have / We've got** a nice room in the hotel.
Lisa **had** long hair when she was a child.

lesson.heading: Questions and negatives: three possible forms
lesson.note: In past questions and negatives we use did / didn't: Did you have a car when you were living in Paris? I didn't have my phone, so I couldn't call you. Lisa had long hair, didn't she?

lesson.heading: have breakfast / have a shower / have a good time
lesson.text: We also use **have** (but not have got) for things we do or experience: have breakfast / dinner / a cup of coffee / something to eat; a bath / a shower / a swim / a break / a rest / a party / a holiday; an accident / an experience / a dream; a look (at something); a chat / a discussion / a conversation (with somebody); trouble / difficulty / fun / a good time; a baby (= give birth to a baby).

examples.text: Sometimes I **have** (= eat) a sandwich for my lunch.
but **I've got** / I have some sandwiches. Would you like one?
examples.note: here have = possess, so have got is fine

lesson.heading: Continuous forms and do/does/did with these expressions
lesson.text: Because these are actions, you *can* use continuous forms (I'm having etc.) with them. In questions and negative sentences we use **do/does/did**.

examples.text: We're enjoying our holiday. **We're having** a great time.
I **don't usually have** a big breakfast.
**Did you have** trouble finding somewhere to stay?

lesson.text: have got works only for things you possess or are affected by (a car, a sister, a cold, a lesson). If have means eat, take, spend or experience, only have is possible - and there it can be continuous.

pairs.right: She's got no brothers or sisters.

pairs.left: You've got a really good voice.
pairs.right: I wish I could sing as well as you.

pairs.left: I don't feel very well this morning.

pairs.right: She's got a degree in physics.

exercises.prompt: Can you say have got here, or only have?
Is there anything you'd like to ask? ___ any questions?
exercises.explanation: Present question about possession: Do you have ... ? or Have you got ... ?

exercises.prompt: We got wet in the rain yesterday. We ___ an umbrella.
exercises.explanation: Past negative uses didn't have (not hadn't got).

exercises.statement: Lisa had got long hair when she was a child.
exercises.explanation: Lisa had long hair when she was a child. In the past we use had, not had got.
Have a shower is an action, so the continuous is possible and have got is not: He's having a shower.

exercises.prompt: Jack ___ a car. He can't afford one and he can't drive anyway.
exercises.explanation: Present negative for possession: doesn't have or hasn't got.

exercises.statement: 'Are you feeling OK?' 'No, I'm having a cold.'
exercises.explanation: No, I have a cold. or I've got a cold. An illness is a state, so no continuous form.

exercises.statement: Was your trip OK? Had you any problems?
exercises.explanation: Did you have any problems? Past questions with have use did; Had you ... ? is unusual.

exercises.prompt: Joe is away on holiday at the moment. I hope he ___.
exercises.explanation: Have a nice time is an experience, so the continuous form is used for now: he's having a nice time.

exercises.statement: I'm not working right now. I'm having a break.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Have a break is an action, so the continuous form I'm having is fine.

exercises.prompt: I'd like to go away somewhere. I ___ for a long time.
exercises.explanation: Present perfect of have a holiday: I haven't had a holiday for a long time.
